No. 25-417

In the Supreme Court of the United States
FRANCIS NIELSEN, PETITIONER,
v.
KEKAI WATANABE, RESPONDENT.
ON WRIT OF CERTIORARI TO THE
UNITED STATES COURT OF APPEALS
FOR THE NINTH CIRCUIT
BRIEF OF AMICI CURIAE  PROFESSORS
JAMES E. PFANDER AND ALEXANDER A.
REINERT SUPPORTING RESPONDENT

R. STANTON JONES
ANDREW T. TUTT
Counsel of Record
TRIAL LAWYERS FOR JUSTICE
421 W. Water Street
Decorah, IA 52101
(866) 854-5529
Andrew@TL4J.com

(i)
TABLE OF CONTENTS
Page
Interests of Amici Curiae ................................................... 1

I. Bivens remedies are statutory precedents and
should be treated that way. ......................................... 3

distinguished into oblivion. ........................................ 17

(1)
INTERESTS OF AMICI CURIAE
Amici are law professors who study constitutional
remedies and federal jurisdiction. They submit this brief
to explain why established Bivens remedies deserve the
protection of statutory stare decisis and must be given fair
effect.1
James E. Pfander is the Owen L. Coon Professor of
Law at Northwestern Pritzker School of Law. Alexander
A. Reinert is the Max Freund Professor of Litigation and
Advocacy at Benjamin N. Cardozo School of Law, Yeshiva
University. Their scholarship addresses constitutional
litigation and official accountability.
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
The important thing to understand about Bivens and
Carlson is that they are statutory precedents. That fact is
too often obscured in discussions about whether and when
those precedents should be extended. As statutory
precedents, they implicate the principle of stare decisis
that governs other statutory precedents, and they trigger
this Court’s acknowledged obligation not to unduly
narrow them and to accord them greater stare decisis
respect than constitutional precedents receive. Petitioner
asks this Court to ignore this insight and do something
that the Court would almost never do to a precedent
interpreting a statute: overrule it in all but name. The
Court does not do that in statutory cases for a simple
reason: When the Court creates a moving target with its
precedents it makes it impossible for Congress to legislate

1 No counsel for a party authored this brief in whole or  in part. No

other than amici or their counsel made such a monetary

2

around the Court’s decisions. And indeed, the Court’s
constant revisions to the “extent” and the “scope” of the
Bivens remedies have had just that effect. Congress has
enacted laws in reliance on these precedents only to have
the precedents eroded, and with them the careful
compromises upon which Congress legislated.
These precedents should be read as this Court reads
any other statutory precedent. Under that approach,
everyone knows exactly what a Carlson claim is: it is an
Eighth Amendment claim for deliberate indifference to a
serious medical need. It is just like its cousin, the
deliberate-indifference claim under 42 U.S.C. § 1983. Its
reach is the same. Its damages remedy is the same. Its
qualified-immunity regime is the same. Butz v.
Economou, 438 U.S. 478, 504 (1978); Wilson v. Layne, 526
U.S. 603, 609 (1999). It really is that simple.
Applied fairly, Carlson governs this case. Courts
must assess the defendants’ roles, the challenged conduct,
the governing obligations, and any distinct institutional
concerns. But Carlson’s asthma, inoperative respirator,
and death describe the facts of that case; they do not
confine its holding to an identical tragedy. A court will
have to determine whether respondent can demonstrate
deliberate indifference to medical needs, but Carlson
already established that respondent has a right to sue for
that constitutional violation. Here, petitioner’s
distinctions concerning diagnosis, severity, and available
remedies do not make this medical-care claim
meaningfully different from Carlson. The Court should
apply the rule it established and Congress built upon. The
judgment should be affirmed.

3

ARGUMENT
I. BIVENS REMEDIES ARE STATUTORY PRECEDENTS
AND SHOULD BE TREATED THAT WAY.
The established Bivens remedies enforce
constitutional rights through judicially fashioned
remedies grounded in statutory authority and subject to
congressional revision. Once recognized, those remedies
warrant the heightened stare decisis protection afforded
statutory precedents for the same reasons that protection
attaches to any other statutory precedent. Congress may
choose to revise them or it may choose to build on or
around them, and absent special justification the Court
should step back and allow Congress to make those
choices. The Court retains its role in interpreting the
Constitution and defining the elements of the
constitutional violation. But the question here is whether
a damages cause of action exists, not how the underlying
constitutional right should be defined. The separation-ofpowers principles that counsel against creating new
remedies also counsel against dismantling remedies
Congress has known about for decades and intentionally
preserved.
Start first with Bivens’ roots in statutory authority.
The Court understood Congress’s grant of federalquestion jurisdiction in 28 U.S.C. § 1331 to authorize
courts to enforce the Constitution through traditional
remedies, including damages. That understanding is
contestable. But if it was mistaken, the mistake was one
of statutory interpretation. See Bush v. Lucas, 462 U.S.
367, 378 (1983); Bivens v. Six Unknown Named Agents of
Federal Bureau of Narcotics , 403 U.S. 388, 405 (1971)
(Harlan, J., concurring in the judgment). That commonlaw method implemented the remedial authority the
Court understood Congress to have conferred through
§ 1331. Bush, 462 U.S. at 378. As Pfander and Baltmanis
put it, Bivens fashioned “a federal common law right of

4

action to enforce the Fourth Amendment.” James E.
Pfander & David Baltmanis, Rethinking Bivens:
Legitimacy and Constitutional Adjudication , 98 Geo.
L.J. 117, 117 (2009). The Court has continued to describe
the inquiry in common-law terms even when it declines to
recognize a remedy. Wilkie v. Robbins, 551 U.S. 537, 554
(2007) (the question calls for “weighing reasons for and
against the creation of a new cause of action, the way
common law judges have always done”). The upshot is
that the Court has grounded its common law Bivens
doctrine in an understanding of the authority conferred
on the judiciary via statute.
These are therefore statutory precedents: they settle
the scope of a statutory grant of remedial authority. Their
construction should endure on the same terms as other
statutory precedents. A judicial reading of a statute
carries a “strong presumption of continued validity.”
Square D Co. v. Niagara Frontier Tariff Bureau, Inc. ,
476 U.S. 409, 424 (1986); accord Neal v. United States, 516
U.S. 284, 295 (1996) (“Once we have determined a
statute’s meaning, we adhere to our ruling under the
doctrine of stare decisis”). Statutory stare decisis protects
even judicially developed doctrines implementing a
statute, because Congress retains authority to revise
them. Kimble v. Marvel Entertainment, LLC , 576 U.S.
446, 456 (2015). A later Court’s disagreement with the
method that produced the rule does not, by itself, justify
undoing it, and that is especially so for statutory law. Id.
at 455-456. Franklin v. Gwinnett County Public Schools
applied the same reasoning to remedies under a judicially
implied action, reading later legislation as “a validation of
Cannon’s holding.” 503 U.S. 60, 72 (1992). This Court has
already applied that logic to Bivens itself, describing
“[t]he settled law of Bivens in this common and recurrent
sphere of law enforcement, and the undoubted reliance
upon it as a fixed principle in the law,” as “powerful

5

reasons to retain it in that sphere.” Ziglar v. Abbasi, 582
U.S. 120, 134 (2017).
The government argues that Carlson relied on the
Constitution rather than federal common law. U.S. Br. 29.
That is incorrect. And the premise matters, because once
a construction is statutory the Court has ordinarily left its
correction to Congress even when the Court thinks the
construction wrong. Ramos v. Louisiana, 590 U.S. 83, 119
(2020) (Kavanaugh, J., concurring in part); Allen v.
Milligan, 599 U.S. 1, 39 (2023). Bush v. Lucas explained
that statutory federal-question jurisdiction supplies
authority to award constitutional damages through
common-law adjudication, subject to congressional
direction and special factors counseling restraint. 462 U.S.
at 378. Carlson v. Green  accordingly recognized
Congress’s power to substitute another remedy. 446 U.S.
14, 18-19 (1980). Even Hernández v. Mesa  describes the
Court’s later change in approach as a demand for clearer
congressional intent than Justice Harlan had inferred
from § 1331. 589 U.S. 93, 101 (2020). The dispute here thus
concerns what Congress authorized, and any error lies in
this Court’s own construction of that statutory authority
in Bivens and Carlson. Congress can correct that
construction; it cannot revise the Constitution. That
distinction supplies the reason for heightened statutory
stare decisis, and it applies even if the Court would
construe the same grant of statutory authority more
narrowly today.
Recognizing the statutory ground for Bivens
remedies carries with it an important corollary:
Preserving a precedent requires giving it fair effect.
Imagine a federal statute authorizing recovery for
deliberate indifference to serious medical needs. Courts
could not fairly interpret that statute to cover only
asthma, only a particular failure of medical equipment, or
only neglect ending in death. Nor could they treat

6

Congress’s imposition of exhaustion requirements as
silently eliminating the action those requirements
regulate. No rational Congress creates conditions
precedent for a legal claim that the legislature intends to
eradicate entirely. Those constructions would be
recognized for what they are: attempts to defeat an
established rule through artificial distinctions, if not
outright distortions. They are no more legitimate when
the rule originates in statutory common law.
A precedent governs more than cases with identical
facts. A holding of this Court reaches beyond the
particular events that produced it; otherwise, this Court
could not ensure the like treatment of like cases . That is
why Carlson claims extend to all cases of medical neglect
that are not meaningfully different from a standard-issue
deliberate-indifference-to-medical-need claim. Merely
cataloguing factual differences does not—cannot—suffice
to make a difference meaningful or genuine. The view that
the Court was wrong to set a precedent is not a good and
sufficient reason to refuse to apply it to a case it plainly
reaches.
The government, for its part, disagrees. But whether
its position stems from a genuine commitment to
separation-of-powers principles rather than a bare desire
to escape accountability is open to question. It has after
all been hostile to accountability for its misconduct since
before Bivens and seemingly will remain so for the
foreseeable future—even in the face of clear statutory
language to the contrary . See, e.g., Thacker v. TVA , 587
U.S. 218, 223-226 (2019) (rejecting the Government’s
request to read a discretionary-function exception into the
TVA’s sue-and- be-sued clause); United States v. Kwai
Fun Wong , 575 U.S. 402, 417-420 (2015) (rejecting the
argument that the Federal Tort Claims Act’s time limits
are jurisdictional because they condition a waiver of
sovereign immunity). Thus, the government says the

7

Court can simply declare Carlson “moribund” while
insisting that this requires no change to existing doctrine.
U.S. Br. 24-25. That is overruling in substance, and it
should not be lightly undertaken. It requires the
justification due a decision to overrule a statutory
precedent Congress has built upon.
There is a difference in law and life between a refusal
to extend a precedent and a refusal to erase it. Perhaps
the Court would decline to recognize the cause of action
announced in Carlson today. But that is not a good reason
to deny that decision its effect while professing to retain
it.
II. THE COURT SHOULD RESPECT CONGRESS’ CHOICE
TO BUILD ON THESE STATUTORY PRECEDENTS.
The reasons to afford Bivens and Carlson special
stare decisis respect are stronger even than they are for
ordinary statutory precedents because Congress built
later statutes on them . As explained above, the Court
understood § 1331’s grant of federal-question jurisdiction
to authorize judicial enforcement of the Constitution
through damages. Congress then legislated around the
actions the Court recognized in the 1974 intentional-tort
amendments to the Federal Tort Claims Act (FTCA), the
1988 Westfall Act, and the 1996 Prison Litigation Reform
Act (PLRA). Erasing Carlson now not only unwinds a
statutory precedent, it unwinds the operation of
Congress’s later laws that were built on it.
The legislative record is not ambiguous. Congress has
legislated against the backdrop of Bivens and Carlson
over and over again.
The 1974 FTCA amendments.  When Congress
extended the FTCA to intentional torts by federal lawenforcement officers, the Senate Report called the
provision “a counterpart to the Bivens case and its
progen[y], in that it waives the defense of sovereign

8

immunity so as to make the Government independently
liable in damages for the same type of conduct that is
alleged to have occurred in Bivens.” S. Rep. No. 93-588,
at 3 (1973), quoted in Carlson, 446 U.S. at 20 (emphasis
supplied). Victims of such raids, the Report explained,
“will have a cause of action against the individual Federal
agents and the Federal Government.” Id. Congress
placed a remedy alongside Bivens; it did not substitute
one for it.
The Westfall Act.  In 1988, Congress expressly
preserved constitutional damages actions when it
displaced overlapping common-law tort suits against
federal employees. The Westfall Act substituted the
United States as the defendant for common-law tort
claims made actionable under the FTCA and arising from
employees’ conduct within the scope of their employment.
Its declared purpose was “to protect Federal employees
from personal liability for common law torts committed
within the scope of their employment.” Pub. L. No. 100-
694, § 2(b), 102 Stat. 4563, 4564. Congress accomplished
that purpose by making the FTCA remedy against the
United States exclusive of claims against the employee by
reason of the same subject matter and precluding other
related civil actions against the employee, but expressly
excepted actions “brought for a violation of the
Constitution of the United States.” Id. § 5; 28 U.S.C. §
2679(b)(2)(A). The distinction was deliberate. As the
House Report explained, “[c]ourts have drawn a sharp
distinction between common law torts and constitutional
or Bivens torts,” and the Act’s exclusive remedy
“expressly does not extend” to the latter. H.R. Rep. No.
100-700, at 6 (1988).
The bill’s proponents repeatedly confirmed that
existing Bivens actions would survive. On passage,
Senator Grassley emphasized that it “does not have any
effect on the so-called Bivens cases or constitutional tort

9

claims,” which “can continue to be brought against
individual Government officials.” 134 Cong. Rec. 29,933
(1988). He made substantially the same statement when
he introduced the Senate bill. Id. at 14,266. The
Department of Justice likewise told the Senate that the
Westfall “fix” “in no way addresses the question of Bivens
Constitutional actions; those remain a separate subject to
be addressed separately.” Department of Justice
Authorization for Fiscal Year 1989 (Civil, Criminal, and
Civil Rights Divisions): Hearings Before the S. Comm.
on the Judiciary, 100th Cong., pt. 2, at 4 (1988) (statement
of John R. Bolton, Ass’t Att’y Gen., Civil Div.). Congress
thus did more than leave Bivens unaddressed: it expressly
preserved the established constitutional actions as part of
the remedial scheme it enacted.
The PLRA. Congress likewise legislated on the
understanding that federal prisoners could bring Bivens
actions when it enacted the PLRA, imposing an
exhaustion requirement on that existing remedy.
Representative LoBiondo, who sponsored the federalprisoner exhaustion proposal in H.R. 2468, expressly
identified the decision Congress sought to change:
McCarthy v. Madigan, which held that a federal prisoner
seeking only money damages could bring a Bivens action
without first exhausting administrative remedies. 141
Cong. Rec. 35,623 (1995). He explained that McCarthy
had been decided “without the benefit of any legislative
guidance,” with the Court “almost to the point of asking
that Congress do something.” Id. His bill supplied that
guidance by making clear “that administrative exhaustion
be imposed in all actions arising under the Bivens case.”
Id. Discussing the conference proposal, he further
confirmed that he had worked with the conferees “to
ensure that the prison litigation reform measures address
the Bivens issue.” Id.

10

The provision’s stated rationale presupposed that
meritorious Bivens claims would continue. LoBiondo
quoted former Attorney General Thornburgh’s
explanation that exhaustion would filter out frivolous
claims, so that “only those claims with a greater
probability/magnitude of success would, presumably,
proceed.” Id. at 35,624. Congress thus imposed a
procedural prerequisite on an established cause of action,
making prisoners exhaust administrative remedies before
pursuing the remedy Congress understood they already
possessed.
Treaty obligations. The Senate also relied on Bivens
and Carlson in determining that existing federal law
supplied the remedies required by international treaties.
In recommending consent to the Convention Against
Torture, the Senate Foreign Relations Committee’s
report reproduced the Executive Branch’s explanation
that no new compensation legislation was necessary
because “[e]xisting U.S. law already establishes private
rights of suit sufficient to implement Article 14,” including
“a suit for constitutional tort.” S. Exec. Rep. No. 101-30,
at 11, 24 (1990). It specifically cited Bivens and Carlson.
Id. The Committee’s report on the Racial Discrimination
Convention reproduced the same understanding: that
“[f]ederal officials may be sued for damages directly
under provisions of the Constitution,” followed by a
citation to Bivens. S. Exec. Rep. No. 103-29, at 9, 17-18
(1994). The Senate thus treated these remedies as an
existing means of satisfying the Nation’s treaty
obligations—the very remedies petitioner now asks this
Court to render ineffective. See James E. Pfander,
Constitutional Torts and the War on Terror 107-11 (2017)
(discussing implementation of Convention Against
Torture).
Proposals to replace or codify the remedy.
Members of Congress have repeatedly proposed

11

legislation to change the constitutional damages remedy,
treating its scope and availability as matters within
Congress’s control. Beginning in the 1970s, Members
introduced bills to replace the action against individual
officers with a remedy against the United States. Senator
Grassley’s S. 1775, for example, would have amended title
28 “to provide for an exclusive remedy against the United
States in suits based upon acts or omissions of U.S.
employees, [and] to provide a remedy against the United
States with respect to constitutional torts.” 127 Cong.
Rec. 25,341 (1981). He described the bill as “a continuation
of efforts made in the previous two Congresses,”
prompted by the “exponential increase” in suits following
Bivens. Id. Those proposals did not become law. When
Congress enacted the Westfall Act seven years later, it
expressly excepted constitutional claims, and Senator
Grassley confirmed that the Act left Bivens untouched.
More recent proposals would expressly codify a damages
action against federal officials. The Bivens Act would
amend 42 U.S.C. § 1983 to reach persons acting under the
authority “of the United States or” of any State. H.R.
6091, 119th Cong. § 2 (2025); see also S. 3187, 119th Cong.
(2025). Those proposals likewise have not become law.
Their significance is limited but consistent: Members
have sought both to replace the judicially recognized
remedy and to place it on an express statutory footing,
invoking Congress’s authority to make either choice. This
Court has drawn the same inference from the same kind
of record. After Kiowa Tribe of Okla. v. Manufacturing
Technologies, Inc. , 523 U.S. 751 (1998), Congress
considered bills broadly curtailing tribal sovereign
immunity, declined to adopt them, and enacted “a far
more modest alternative” instead; the Court treated that
choice as an “initial . . . decision to retain” the immunity,
and declined to overrule. Michigan v. Bay Mills Indian
Community, 572 U.S. 782, 801, 803 (2014). The inference
is strongest, the Court explained, where Congress took up

12

the question “partly at our urging.” Id. at 803. Congress
took up this one at the Court’s urging as well. See Carlson,
446 U.S. at 52-53 (Rehnquist, J., dissenting) (Congress is
“free to devise whatever remedy it sees fit” and to have it
“altogether displace” the action recognized that day). The
Court should respect the choices Congress actually
enacted in the meantime.
That history answers the government’s effort to
characterize Carlson as a constitutional rather than
statutory precedent. U.S. Br. 29. For half a century,
Congress has proceeded on the understanding that the
Bivens remedy is subject to legislative control. Members
have proposed replacing it or expressly codifying it;
Congress has enacted laws supplementing, preserving,
and regulating it. Three statutes, enacted by three
different Congresses, reflect the same premise: the action
exists, Congress may prescribe its operation, and
Congress has chosen to build on it. That is the ordinary
life of a statutory precedent—and a powerful reason to
afford it the stability statutory stare decisis protects.
The Westfall Act makes the point concrete. Congress
made the FTCA remedy “exclusive of any other civil
action or proceeding for money damages by reason of the
same subject matter against the employee whose act or
omission gave rise to the claim,” then expressly excepted
actions “brought for a violation of the Constitution of the
United States.” 28 U.S.C. § 2679(b)(1), (2)(A); see James
E. Pfander & Rex N. Alley, Federal Tort Liability After
Egbert v. Boule: The Case for Restoring the Officer Suit
at Common Law, 138 Harv. L. Rev. 985, 1036-38 (2025).
That exception reflects a legislative choice to preserve
constitutional damages actions within a remedial system
Congress had authority to reshape. If the Constitution
itself compelled those actions, their survival would not
depend on Congress’s exception. Congress instead
legislated around the continued availability of Bivens and

13

Carlson, expressly preserving them while displacing
other officer suits. The Court should not erase by
construction the precedents on which that statutory
arrangement rests.
Erasing Carlson would undo one part of that
legislative arrangement while leaving the other intact. As
Pfander, Reinert, and Schwartz explain, Congress
displaced the ordinary common-law action against the
employee while preserving any government liability
under the FTCA and constitutional liability under Bivens.
James E. Pfander, Alexander A. Reinert & Joanna C.
Schwartz, The Myth of Personal Liability: Who Pays
When Bivens Claims Succeed , 72 Stan. L. Rev. 561, 574
(2020). Eliminating Carlson would withdraw the
constitutional remedy Congress preserved without
restoring any officer suits Congress displaced. The result
would alter Congress’s chosen remedial scheme: the
statutory restriction on officer liability would remain, but
an established action Congress expressly left available
would disappear.2
To be sure, Hernández, 589 U.S. at 111 n.9, rejected
using that exception to authorize an extension of Bivens.
The exception “simply left Bivens where it found it.” But
this case is not Hernández. Unlike Hernández, this is not
a case about extending anything, this is a case about
where, exactly Congress “found” Bivens when it enacted
the Westfall Act. Leaving an established remedy where
Congress found it is different from extending it to new
claims altogether. Reinert and Mulligan identify the
separation-of-powers problem with disregarding
Congress’s recognition of the remedy when deciding
whether a claim invokes an existing action. Alexander A.

2 The government’s FTCA liability would remain only for
intentional torts committed by law enforcement officer s. See 28
U.S.C. § 2680(h).

14

Reinert & Lumen N. Mulligan, Asking the First
Question: Reframing Bivens after Minneci , 90 Wash. U.
L. Rev. 1473, 1496-1497 (2013). Respect for Congress’s
later statute strengthens the case for retaining the actions
Congress relied on when it enacted it.
The PLRA expanded the exhaustion requirement
from actions under § 1983 to actions under “any other
Federal law,” thereby bringing federal prisoners’ Carlson
suits within its scope. 42 U.S.C. § 1997e(a); Porter v.
Nussle, 534 U.S. 516, 524 (2002). Congress also regulated
claims for monetary relief, requiring dismissal of claims
against immune defendants and restricting recovery for
mental or emotional injury. § 1997e(c)(1), (e). Those
provisions govern other kinds of suits as well, but
Congress enacted them against the backdrop of Carlson,
imposing conditions on an existing remedy without
eliminating it. Although Ziglar v. Abbasi , 582 U.S. 120,
149 (2017), characterized Porter’s statement as dictum, it
suggested merely that Congress’s failure to create a
standalone damages remedy might counsel against
extending Carlson to other forms of prisoner
mistreatment. That concern about extending Carlson
does not undermine the inference that Congress tacitly
recognized the remedy Carlson already supplied when it
expanded the PLRA’s exhaustion scheme to regulate it.3
The government argues that the Westfall Act is
neutral toward Bivens and that the PLRA never names
Carlson. U.S. Br. 28-29. But leaving an existing remedy
intact while rejecting extensions is a legislative choice
following a statutory interpretation decision by this

3 Once again, it is unclear how the government can sq uare its claim
that Carlson claims are constitutional in nature (U.S. Br. 29) w ith
Congress’s decision to impose an exhaustion requireme nt as a
precondition to such claims. Congress, plainly, has always viewed
these claims as subconstitutional law capable of reg ulation by
statute.

15

Court, and here Congress did better than that. The
PLRA’s exhaustion requirement answered McCarthy v.
Madigan, 503 U.S. 140 (1992), which held that a federal
prisoner need not exhaust administrative remedies before
bringing a Bivens action seeking only money damages.
503 U.S. at 149. The sponsor of the exhaustion provision
said so on the floor. 141 Cong. Rec. 35,623 (1995)
(statement of Rep. LoBiondo). Congress need not say
“this statute is designed to regulate Carlson claims” to
have intentionally done exactly that.
Along similar lines, the Court has treated
congressional acceptance of the settled Rule 10b-5 action
as a reason to retain it while leaving its expansion to
Congress. Stoneridge Investment Partners, LLC v.
Scientific-Atlanta, Inc. , 552 U.S. 148, 165-166 (2008).
Congress should be able to legislate on the understanding
that, absent special justification, settled statutory
constructions will remain law until Congress decides to
change them. Kimble, 576 U.S. at 456. Otherwise, the
Court can unintentionally undermine a later legislative
choice by erasing an earlier rule on which Congress relied.
Following this Court’s approach in Stoneridge, then,
Congress can be seen as having accepted a judge-made
private cause of action “as then defined” and having
chosen to “extend it no further.” 552 U.S. at 166. Such a
conclusion appears to have informed this Court’s
approach in Ziglar v. Abbasi , which established the
current two-step framework for the analysis of the
viability of a suit under Bivens. As Ziglar explained,
following the approach in Stoneridge, the Bivens doctrine
was to be understood as extending only to the contexts
previously settled by decisions of this Court. The Ziglar
Court therefore affirmed the viability of the Bivens
doctrine in what this Court called the “common and
recurrent sphere of law enforcement.” 582 U.S. at 134.
But in new contexts—those that Congress had not

16

implicitly reaffirmed in the Westfall Act and the PLRA—
Bivens actions were subject to a searching special factors
analysis. Recognizing that Congress was to take the lead
in expanding the right to sue and had failed to do so in the
PLRA, the same reasoning applies here: Congress
accepted the settled rights to sue and went no further. Or,
as the Court put it in an echo of Stoneridge, it “could be
argued” that the PLRA “suggests Congress chose not to
extend the Carlson damages remedy to cases involving
other types of prisoner mistreatment.” 582 U.S. at 149.
Widespread reliance on Bivens and Carlson is not an
abstract matter. Congress supplemented the Bivens
remedy in 1974 without displacing it, extending the FTCA
to intentional torts by federal law-enforcement officers.
Pub. L. No. 93-253, 88 Stat. 50 (codified at 28 U.S.C. §
2680(h)). The Senate Report called that provision “a
counterpart to the Bivens case and its progen[y],” and
this Court quoted it. Carlson, 446 U.S. at 20. Abbasi
recognized that Bivens guides officers and supplies a
fixed legal principle on which others rely. 582 U.S. at 134.
Its express assurance concerned Bivens’s search-andseizure context, but the institutional reasoning applies to
Carlson too. Congress, courts, officers, and prisoners
have operated within a remedial system that includes the
medical-care action. Petitioner attacks Bivens’s original
reasoning, Pet. Br. 40-48, and answers the reliance point
by asserting that congressional reliance is “precisely the
problem,” Pet. Br. 47. That answer has it backwards. The
separation-of-powers objection to judicially created
remedies is that they displace Congress’s judgment;
withdrawing this remedy would displace the statutes
Congress actually enacted around it. The separation of
powers supplies a reason both to preserve the remedy and
not to expand it. There is no contradiction there.

17

III. CARLSON SHOULD BE FAIRLY APPLIED, NOT
DISTINGUISHED INTO OBLIVION.
Eliminating an action Congress recognized, accepted,
and built on requires more than pointing out that the
Court would not create it today. But the government asks
exactly that: it argues that the Court should declare
Carlson moribund while reserving broader
reconsideration of Bivens. U.S. Br. 3, 23-28. Its position is
categorical: no future prisoner case can invoke Carlson.
U.S. Br. 24-25. How is that not overruling Carlson? The
government first insists that recognizing Carlson’s
obsolescence requires no change in doctrine, then offers
an alternative stare decisis analysis. U.S. Br. 25-28.
Neither route answers the statutory stare decisis
argument.
To give statutory precedents appropriate stare
decisis effect, the meaningful-difference inquiry must
preserve an established remedy’s fair scope. Lower
courts must follow directly applicable precedent even
when later decisions appear to undermine its reasoning,
leaving overruling to this Court. Rodriguez de Quijas v.
Shearson/American Express, Inc. , 490 U.S. 477, 484
(1989). Restrictions on extensions must be applied
together with the holdings that remain binding.
Abbasi asks whether a case differs from an
established context in a meaningful way. 582 U.S. at 139-
140. Its comparison includes the constitutional right,
officers’ roles, challenged conduct, legal obligations,
judicial guidance, institutional disruption, and previously
unconsidered special factors. Even a modest extension is
an extension. Id. at 147. But some differences are too
trivial to create a new context. Id. at 149. Courts must
explain why the identified difference changes the
remedial question.
Petitioner says every single case must consider anew
whether Congress could imagine a difference relevant to

18

authorizing liability. Pet. Br. 23- 24. That of course is
tantamount to saying that merely applying Carlson is the
same thing as extending it, because Congress could
distinguish virtually any two injuries or encounters. That
legislative freedom does not mean that applying a
precedent to nonidentical facts automatically creates a
new action. The question is whether the identified
difference places the claim outside the medical-care
context Carlson recognized.
Here the question whether this is a heartland Carlson
claim is not a close one. Carlson concerned officials’
alleged deliberate indifference to a federal prisoner’s
serious medical needs: hours of inadequate attention,
contraindicated drugs, a broken respirator, and delayed
hospital transfer, followed by death. 446 U.S. at 16 n.1. In
this case, on review of a pleading-stage dismissal, the
court of appeals described allegations that Nielsen
refused hospital treatment despite Watanabe’s reports of
severe pain after an assault by other inmates; a fractured
coccyx was diagnosed seven months later. Pet. App. 3a-
5a.
Petitioner seizes on the single encounter with Nielsen
and the absence of a life-threatening emergency as
distinctions between Carlson and this case; he adds (while
calling the points immaterial) that Nielsen is a paramedic
and did provide some treatment. Pet. Br. 12 n.7, 13, 29-32
& n.11. Those matters bear on whether he was
deliberately indifferent. They do not by themselves
change this from a case at Carlson’s core: a claim against
an individual federal prison medical provider for
deliberately disregarding a prisoner’s serious medical
need.
Death is not an element of the Carlson action.
Petitioner emphasizes that the estate in Carlson could not
seek prospective relief, and the government invokes the
Court’s concern with state survivorship rules. Pet. Br. 25-

19

26, 38; U.S. Br. 21. Those remedial features deserve
consideration, but they do not make death an element of
the action. Carlson’s concern that state law might defeat
the estate’s recovery led the Court to adopt a uniform
federal rule of survivorship. 446 U.S. at 23-25. It did not
hold that a prisoner’s survival defeats the otherwise
established medical-care action.
Alternative remedies require the same discipline.
They can bear on context: Abbasi expressly considered
potential special factors, alternative relief, and the PLRA.
582 U.S. at 139-140, 148-149. Egbert v. Boule holds that an
alternative structure can foreclose a new action even
without judicial review or equivalent relief. 596 U.S. 482,
497-498 (2022). But deciding whether to create an action
remains different from applying one already recognized.
The FTCA cannot supply a basis for narrowing Carlson
when Carlson itself held that the FTCA and the
constitutional damages action could coexist. 446 U.S. at
19-23.
Petitioner admits that the Bureau of Prisons’
Administrative Remedy Program existed when Carlson
was decided, but stresses that the Court did not consider
it and that neither the inmate nor his estate could use it.
Pet. Br. 18-19, 37-38. But so what? Treating the grievance
process and the PLRA as reasons every medical-care
claim is new would eliminate the action across the board,
thereby undermining the judgment of the political
branches that enacted and signed the PLRA. The
exhaustion provision would becom e a reason to void the
very relief that exhaustion provision was supposed to
regulate. That counterintuitive consequence does not
follow from the statute’s command to exhaust.
The Court’s own formulation points against
petitioner’s argument . Abbasi said that “[i]t could be
argued” that the PLRA suggests Congress chose not to
extend Carlson to “other types of prisoner

20

mistreatment.” 582 U.S. at 149. And Goldey v. Fields, 606
U.S. 942, 943-945 (2025) (per curiam) declined to
recognize a new prisoner excessive-force action in light of
congressional legislation, administrative remedies, and
institutional concerns. But, though they certainly could
have, neither decision abrogated the established medicalcare action for Eighth Amendment deliberate
indifference to serious medical needs. Restricting new
kinds of claims gives those decisions effect; narrowing
Carlson to the point of extinguishing it does far more.
The government’s reliance on Cisco Systems, Inc. v.
Doe I, 146 S. Ct. 1882 (2026), is misplaced. U.S. Br. 24-25.
In rejecting new Alien Tort Statute actions, Cisco
emphasized that this Court had never itself created one.
146 S. Ct. at 1892. Yet it left undisturbed the assumed
availability of actions for three historical torts, expressly
considering possible litigant reliance. Id. at 1892 & n.3.
Carlson is an actual decision recognizing an action.
Holding that no new claims should be recognized under
the ATS is not a reason to overrule statutory precedents
upholding the right to pursue claims in what this Court
has described as “settled contexts.”
The Court should apply Carlson’s established
medical-care action, leaving the merits and defenses for
adjudication. If it chooses to consider the view that
Carlson should be overruled, it should confront overruling
it under the standard that governs overruling a statutory
precedent that Congress has built upon. Giving effect to
Congress’s power to make the laws requires respecting
the fixed constructions on which they rest.

21

CONCLUSION
The judgment of the court of appeals should be
affirmed.
